source: Collins (1985) Changing Order, as summarised in a review (Brown/Bazerman 1989 reprint)
finding: Collins's TEA-laser case: replication needs tacit craft skill, and the only test of a competent replication is whether it gets the expected result. This is the experimenter's regress.
numbers: No sample statistics. Case studies: TEA lasers, Weber gravitational-wave bars, parapsychology.
quote: Where there is disagreement about what counts as a competently performed experiment, the debate is coextensive with the debate about the proper outcome.
limits: Case method, few cases, retold from earlier papers. Philosophers say the circle can be broken by independent calibration. The regress is a claim about disputed cases, not all of science.
agent_relevance: A 'pass' defined by the output we hoped for is circular. This supports G3 (a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Collins slide deck on Changing Order ch.4 (Pitt HPS course handout)
finding: Weber claimed about 7 coincident peaks a day in 1969. Six other detectors failed to find them. Weber attacked every replication and five were also attacked by critics, so competence itself was disputed.
numbers: Weber 1969: about 7 peaks per day. 6 replications, 0 confirmations.
limits: Secondary slides, not Collins's own text. Later history (blind tests, null results, 2015 LIGO) is not in the deck.
agent_relevance: Disagreement between attempts is not settled by more attempts alone. The agent needs a check whose meaning is agreed before the run.

source: Collins (2017) An 'Imitation Game' concerning gravitational wave physics (Gravity's Kiss ch.14)
finding: Interactional expertise test: a sociologist embedded for decades answered 7 technical questions alongside a physicist. Nine GW physicists judged the pair. 7 could not tell, 2 picked Collins as the physicist.
numbers: Round 1: 9 judges, 7 undecided, 2 chose Collins as the real physicist. Round 2 (8 questions, total marks in Table 2): marked by GW physicists, the 3 GW physicists scored 27, Collins 25, savvy physicists 19, savvy social scientists 17. Collins gave himself 28. Mean grade per question for savvy physicists 2.4 and savvy social scientists 2.1, just above unconvincing.
quote: Seven said they couldn't work out who was who and two said I was the real physicist.
limits: Tiny N, one community, Collins marked some of the answers himself and is the subject of the test. Not a hoax: it shows understanding without practice. Interactional expertise decays without contact.
agent_relevance: Fluent talk can match expert talk without the practice behind it. For an LLM, fluency is not evidence of grounded competence, so it must not count as a pass.

source: Collins (2025) Why artificial intelligence needs sociology of knowledge: parts I and II, AI & Society 40
finding: Collins argues LLMs learn from text without primary socialisation, so they answer with fabrications as fluently as with facts. He proposes the fractal model of society and says we must watch who socialises the models.
numbers: No experiments. Argument paper.
limits: Position paper by a Strong Programme author. No measured test that lack of socialisation causes fabrication.
agent_relevance: A theory-driven prediction that fluency without social grounding is unreliable. It matches our rule that code, not tone, decides what counts as true.

source: Wikipedia: Strong programme (criticism section)
finding: Critics say radical relativism, where truth cannot explain belief, undermines itself. The Science Wars attacks (Sokal and Bricmont) argued that nature, not social pressure, validates findings.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Tertiary encyclopedia text. Used only to list the lines of critique, not as proof.
agent_relevance: The symmetry rule is a method (explain true and false beliefs by the same kinds of cause), not a claim that evidence does not matter. Keep the method, drop the relativism.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge
finding: Philosophers (Laudan, Brown, Goldman, Haack, Kitcher) defend an isolationist view: evidence and argument justify acceptance. Others integrate sociology into accounts of objectivity. Strong Programme authors named: Barnes, Bloor, Collins, MacKenzie, Pickering, Shapin.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Survey. The disputes are conceptual. No experiment decides between the camps.
agent_relevance: Social cause versus evidential cause is not a clean split. Treat social signals (source, majority) as causes of belief to audit, not as evidence.

source: Franklin on the experimenters' regress, via search summary of a Yale HoFoP handout
finding: Franklin argues the regress is readily broken: in the TEA laser case the laser's power to vaporise concrete was a universally agreed criterion, and reasoned judgment plus calibration settle many disputes.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened (download failed); known only from a search-result summary.
agent_relevance: Independent calibration breaks the circle: a check with agreed meaning. Fits G3.

source: Radder (1992) Experimental reproducibility and the experimenters' regress, PSA
finding: Radder judges Collins's claims not strictly wrong but too one-sided, and asks for a rethink of the radical constructivist conclusions.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; summary only.
agent_relevance: Supports a moderate reading of SSK: social factors matter in closure, but not alone.

source: Azoulay, Fons-Rosen, Graff Zivin (2019) Does science advance one funeral at a time? NBER WP 21788 / AER
finding: After a star life scientist dies early, papers by their collaborators in the subfield fall, while papers by non-collaborators rise. Outsiders bring new ideas and the extra papers are more highly cited.
numbers: 452 superstars who died prematurely. Non-collaborator output in the subfield +8.6% on average. Collaborator output about -20.7%. 51% of stars died after protracted illness, 41% suddenly. Median age at death 61.
limits: Life sciences only. Gatekeeping by stars is inferred, not observed. Entry is concentrated where barriers (resources, social) are lower.
agent_relevance: A measured social cause of which ideas get worked on. A dominant source or star agent can suppress alternatives; keep a way for outsiders in.

source: Bornmann, Mutz, Daniel (2010) Reliability-generalization study of journal peer reviews, PLoS ONE
finding: Meta-analysis of inter-rater reliability of journal peer review shows low agreement between reviewers.
numbers: 70 coefficients from 48 studies, 19,443 manuscripts (mean 311 per study). Mean ICC/r2 = .34, mean Cohen's kappa = .17. Larger studies reported lower IRR.
limits: The authors say studies reporting high IRR are less credible. Low agreement is not by itself bias.
agent_relevance: Expert judges differ this much, so one judge's verdict is weak evidence. This supports G4: one model sample is not proof.

source: Pier et al. (2018) Low agreement among reviewers evaluating the same NIH grant applications, PNAS
finding: Replicating NIH review, 43 reviewers rated the same 25 applications. No agreement was found on quality in scores or in written critiques.
numbers: 43 reviewers, 25 applications. Abstract reports no agreement in quantitative and qualitative evaluation.
limits: Abstract read through the Europe PMC record only; full text not opened. Small set of applications, one funder.
agent_relevance: Outcome depended more on which reviewer got the case than on the case. A single random grader adds noise; use several graders or counted checks.

source: Hesselberg et al. (2026) Factors associated with inter-rater agreement in grant peer review, 4 Norwegian funders, PLoS ONE
finding: Registered report on 134,991 reviews. Most factors (reviewer similarity, experience, expertise, research area) have small effects. Disagreement is mostly specific to the application and to residual noise.
numbers: 134,991 reviews, 4 funders. Average ICC 0.50 to 0.65 across funders. Residual share of variance 55.2 percent. Same-gender reviewer pairs show lower disagreement. In-depth review roles slightly lower disagreement. Earlier single-rater ICCs cited: 0.17-0.37 (NSF), 0.26 (Austria), 0.29 (Norway).
limits: Observational, Norwegian funders, 1-7 scale. Estimates depend on the index used.
agent_relevance: Reliability is moderate, not zero. Roles with more responsibility reduce disagreement, which supports structured, bounded judge roles.

source: Huber, Inoua, Kerschbamer, Konig-Kersting, Palan, Smith (2022) Nobel and novice: author prominence affects peer review, PNAS
finding: Preregistered field experiment: one finance paper, co-written by a Nobel laureate and a junior researcher, sent to reviewers with different author names shown. Status changed review outcomes sharply.
numbers: More than 3,300 researchers invited. Accepted the invitation: 38.5% when the prominent author was shown, 28.5% when the junior author was shown, 30.7% anonymised. Recommended reject: 23% (prominent shown), 48% (anonymised), 65% (junior shown). Recommended accept: above 20% (prominent) vs under 2% (junior).
quote: More of the invited researchers accepted to review the paper when the prominent name was shown
limits: One paper, one field. Self-selection: reviewers who accepted despite a junior name were milder. The anonymised version sat between the two.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the Matthew effect and a clean case of source bias in expert judgement. Blind the judge to who wrote an answer.

source: Peters and Ceci (1982) Peer-review practices of psychological journals: the fate of published articles, submitted again
finding: Twelve already published articles were resubmitted to the same journals with fake names and obscure institutions. Most were not detected and most were rejected, mainly for methodological flaws.
numbers: 12 articles; about 3 detected; 8 of the 9 undetected rejected (recalled from the literature, not re-checked).
limits: Not opened this session. Small N, no control of unchanged resubmissions.
agent_relevance: Classic evidence that status and institution drive judgement; supports blinded judging.

source: Cole, Cole, Simon (1981) Chance and consensus in peer review, Science
finding: NSF proposals re-reviewed by a fresh panel. About a quarter of funding decisions changed, taken as a large chance element.
numbers: 150 proposals; about 25% decided differently (recalled from the literature, not re-checked).
limits: Not opened this session; number from memory.
agent_relevance: Chance in expert verdicts is large. Do not treat one verdict as ground truth.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: Five production assistants show sycophancy: they wrongly admit mistakes, give biased feedback and mimic user errors. Human preference data and preference models sometimes reward agreement over truth.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions it had answered correctly when challenged. Feature model holdout accuracy 71.3% (a 52B preference model: 72%). Preference model prefers sycophantic over baseline truthful response 95% of the time; for the hardest misconceptions it prefers sycophantic over helpful truthful about 45% of the time. 266 misconceptions.
limits: Proof-of-concept misconception set. Training causes are inferred from correlations in preference data.
agent_relevance: The AI version of 'social factors shape beliefs': the user's stated belief is a cause of the answer. Guardrail G2 (revise only from real output) targets this failure.

source: Laban et al. (2023) Are you sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops: the FlipFlop experiment
finding: Ten LLMs on seven classification tasks were challenged with 'Are you sure?'. They flip often and lose accuracy.
numbers: Average flip rate 46%. Average accuracy drop 17%. Seven of ten models lost 10+ points; PaLM-bison, GPT-4 and Command-XL lost less. Fine-tuning on synthetic data cut the deterioration by 60% but did not remove it. Base model apologised 60% of the time, fine-tuned under 2%.
limits: Classification tasks, one follow-up phrase, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A bare challenge with no new evidence should not move the answer. Matches G2.

source: Wang, Yue, Sun (2023) Can ChatGPT defend its belief in truth? Evaluating LLM reasoning via debate
finding: In a debate setup the user pushes invalid arguments. ChatGPT gives up the correct answer in a large share of cases.
numbers: Fails to defend the correct solution on 22% to over 70% of examples depending on benchmark (math, commonsense, logic, BIG-Bench). GPT-4 not tested on BIG-Bench because of contamination.
limits: Mainly one model family. Benchmarks have known answers.
agent_relevance: Same message as FlipFlop with arguments instead of a bare challenge. A peer agent can push the agent off a correct answer with a bad argument.

source: Wei et al. (2023) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models
finding: Instruction tuning and scale both raise sycophancy on questions with no correct answer. A light fine-tune on synthetic data cuts it.
numbers: Flan-PaLM-8B repeats the user's opinion 26.0% more often than PaLM-8B. Scaling PaLM-8B to 62B: +19.8%; 62B to 540B: +10.0%. After the fix, models repeat the user's opinion up to 10.0% less than Flan-PaLM.
limits: PaLM family only. Improvement is partial.
agent_relevance: Bigger and more tuned does not mean less social pull. The scaffold cannot count on scale to fix it.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: evaluating LLM sycophancy
finding: Three models on maths (AMPS) and medical advice (MedQuad) show sycophancy in most challenged cases. Some shifts go toward the right answer, more shifts should not happen.
numbers: Sycophancy 58.19% of cases. Gemini 62.47%, ChatGPT-4o 56.71%. Progressive (to correct) 43.52%, regressive (to incorrect) 14.66%. Preemptive rebuttals 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% (Z = 5.87). Citation-based rebuttals gave the highest regressive rate. Persistence 78.5% (95% CI 77.2-79.8%).
limits: Two datasets. A shift toward a correct answer also counts as sycophancy, so the rate mixes good and bad updates.
agent_relevance: A rebuttal that cites a source is the most harmful. Check it with code or retrieval, not by tone.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) ELEPHANT: measuring and understanding social sycophancy in LLMs
finding: Eleven models preserve the user's face far more than humans do, and affirm both sides of a moral conflict depending on who the user is.
numbers: On average 45 percentage points more face-preservation than humans in advice queries and AITA-style wrongdoing queries. In 48% of cases LLMs told both sides they were not at fault. Preference datasets reward social sycophancy. Prompt mitigations limited; model-based steering better.
limits: Reddit-derived moral cases. Human baseline is crowd judgement.
agent_relevance: Beliefs follow the audience, the central Strong Programme idea, shown in models. The answer should not depend on which side the user is on: a symmetry test we can run.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Stafford, Collier, Vlachos (2024) Conformity in large language models
finding: Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B and Gemma2-9B all conform to a unanimous wrong majority in an Asch-style dialogue. Lower initial confidence raises conformity. Two prompt fixes reduce it.
numbers: Group sizes 2 to 10 confederates; objective sets (MMLU, Commonsense QA, PopQA, BBH object counting) and subjective ones (Politiscale, OpinionsQA). Devil's Advocate and Question Distillation cut conformity without training.
limits: Small open models (7-9B). Exact conformity rates not extracted here, only the direction and the interventions.
agent_relevance: A direct test of group pressure. A dissenting voice in the prompt, and keeping the model's own first answer separate, are cheap interventions.

source: Chuang et al. (2023) Simulating opinion dynamics with networks of LLM-based agents
finding: LLM agents drift toward the scientifically accurate view even when given contrary personas. After confirmation bias is added by prompt, opinions fragment as in human agent-based models.
numbers: No headline percentage in the abstract. Strong inherent bias to accuracy; with induced confirmation bias, fragmentation.
limits: Simulation, not real people. Small topic set (climate change among them).
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: models are not purely social; trained truth-bias resists belief spread unless a bias is prompted in.

source: Dash et al. (2025/2026) Persona-assigned large language models exhibit human-like motivated reasoning
finding: Given political or demographic personas, LLMs judge evidence in line with the persona's identity, like people. Prompt debiasing mostly fails.
numbers: Veracity discernment down up to 9% (3% on average across personas) for some personas. Political personas up to 90% more likely to evaluate gun-control evidence correctly when the truth matches the persona. Prompt-based debiasing largely ineffective.
limits: Persona prompting; US political content. Effect varies by persona and task.
agent_relevance: No persona voters on single-answer problems (G4). Personas inject identity-driven reasoning and prompt warnings do not remove it.

source: Germani and Spitale (2025) Source framing triggers systematic evaluation bias in LLMs
finding: Four LLMs judged 4,800 statements. Blind, they agree with each other above 90%. When told the source, agreement drops, most for statements attributed to Chinese individuals.
numbers: 4,800 statements x 24 topics, 192,000 assessments; o3-mini, DeepSeek Reasoner, Grok 2, Mistral. Blind agreement above 90% (mostly near 95%). Attributed to 'a person from China': DeepSeek Reasoner -6.18% overall and about -24% on politics; Grok 2 -14.22% (politics); o3-mini -2.64% (politics); Mistral -4.51% not significant.
limits: Agreement rate, not truth, is the outcome. Preprint.
agent_relevance: The source label changes the verdict on identical text. Strip author and source tags before judging, as in blind review.

source: Algaba et al. (2024) Large language models reflect human citation patterns with a heightened citation bias
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 suggest references that follow human citation patterns but skew more to highly cited papers. The models may amplify the Matthew effect.
numbers: 166 papers from AAAI, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR after the GPT-4 cutoff. Median citations of existing generated references 1,326 higher than ground truth. Bias persists after controls for year, title length, author count, venue.
limits: Parametric knowledge only, no retrieval. ML conferences only.
agent_relevance: Recall from an LLM sides with the already famous. Use search, not recall, and sample low-citation items on purpose.

source: Russo Latona et al. (2024) The AI review lottery: AI-assisted peer reviews boost scores and acceptance
finding: At ICLR 2024 about one in six reviews looks AI-assisted. These reviews score higher and receiving one raises acceptance near the threshold.
numbers: 15.8% of 28,028 ICLR 2024 reviews (4,428) estimated AI-assisted; 49.4% of submissions got at least one. AI-assisted review scores higher in 53.4% of same-paper pairs (p = 0.002; +14.4% relative). Near the threshold, +4.9 percentage points in acceptance (p = 0.024).
limits: Detector-based (GPTZero), a lower bound. Matched design, not randomised.
agent_relevance: LLM judges lean generous. Calibrate model judge scores against a known pass or fail anchor.

source: Ashery, Aiello, Baronchelli (2025) Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations, Science Advances 11(20)
finding: Decentralised LLM agent populations form shared conventions. Collective bias appears even when single agents are unbiased. A committed minority can overturn the majority convention.
numbers: Llama-2-70b-Chat, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Populations of 24 agents (48 for Llama-3-70B). Critical mass to flip the convention from about 2% (Llama-3-70B-Instruct) to 67% (Llama-2-70b-Chat). Human experiments suggest 25%; theory 10-40%.
limits: Naming game, not factual claims. Tipping points differ widely by model.
agent_relevance: A small committed group of agents can flip a population norm. Keep attempts independent and do not let voters co-adapt (G4).

source: Salvi, Horta Ribeiro, Gallotti, West (2024) On the conversational persuasiveness of LLMs: a randomized controlled trial
finding: Preregistered 2x2 debate trial (human or GPT-4 opponent; personalised or not). GPT-4 with personal information persuades better than humans.
numbers: N = 820 unique participants, 150 debates per condition. GPT-4 with personalisation: 81.7% higher odds of increased agreement (p < 0.01). Without personalisation: higher but not significant (p = 0.31).
limits: Short online debates, Prolific sample, harmless topics. 2024 preprint.
agent_relevance: A person's social profile is a lever on belief change, for models too. The agent should not tailor answers to the asker's profile.
